name: Priya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Priya, I'm 27, and I manage the pig unit at Linden Farm. We've got about 700 sows indoors, and 350 hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes back into the pigs as feed. I run a team of six and I report to the owner, who's in his sixties and happy to let me try things.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six with a walk through the farrowing rooms, where the sows have their piglets, because that's where things go wrong fastest. Then I check the screens: feed use, water, temperatures, and a sound system that listens for coughing. After that it's staff, vet visits, and planning which pigs go to the abattoir on Thursday. At harvest I help on the combine because everyone does. I love the numbers getting better month by month. What wears me out is a disease scare, because one sick pig from outside can shut the whole unit down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a flat in town, and my sister lives two streets away. I use AI every day, for feed plans, staff rotas and reading through vet reports. I got the owner to put in the cough monitor two years ago, before anyone else round here had one. I've got about five months' money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a let-down, honestly. I've got plans for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but oversold, which is true of most new things. The cough monitor saves us real money, the feed planning too. But it's not going to run a pig unit on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be disappointed. I like being the person who brings in the new thing and makes it pay. If that stops, my edge is smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze every bit out of the tools we've got, and write up the cough monitor results to show other farms. I might do some paid consulting on the side, setting up the same system elsewhere. I'd keep saving, maybe look at buying a flat instead of renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit bored. Like a month where every number is just fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Paid consulting. Is that a real idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Two farms have already asked me how we set up the cough monitor. I could charge for a day's visit. It's not big money, but it's a start, and I like showing people things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the owner mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say do what you like as long as the pigs are fine. He's like that. He'd probably be proud, actually.

S0.say: I'd say AI is useful but oversold, like most new things. The cough monitor and feed planning save real money, but they won't run a pig unit on their own.
S0.think: Privately I'd be disappointed. I like being the person who brings in the new thing and makes it pay, and without that my edge is smaller.
S0.do: Gets the most out of existing tools and writes up the cough monitor results for other farms. Starts paid consulting visits to set up similar systems elsewhere, and keeps saving towards buying a flat.
S0.quote: I like being the person who brings in the new thing and makes it pay.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is a confident early adopter who sees the plateau as a loss of opportunity rather than a relief. Even here she spots a side income in consulting. Her employer's trust gives her a lot of freedom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the one I'd bet on, if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so get on with it, but do it carefully. On a pig unit, a mistake with a new system can kill animals. I'd tell people to try it on one room before the whole unit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's great for me. I already know the tools, and farms will need people who can run them. My worry is my team, especially the two who don't like screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in camera systems that weigh pigs and spot fights, and a robot that washes the pens, which is the worst job we have. I'd train my team in the first six months, and I'd grow the consulting into maybe one day a week. I'd put some savings into a short course on farm data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A bit worried for Jakub and Ana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Jakub and Ana.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've been here longer than me and they're brilliant with the sows. Jakub can tell a sow's about to farrow just by how she's lying. But give him a tablet and he goes quiet. I'd want to keep that skill, and I'd have to fight for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pen-washing robot takes the worst job. Who does that job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Ana, with a pressure washer, in the heat and the smell, four hours a day. She'd be glad to see the back of it. But she'd also wonder what she's being kept on for.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming, so get on with it carefully. On a pig unit a mistake with a new system can kill animals, so try it on one room before the whole unit.
S1.think: Privately I think it's great for me, because I already know the tools. My worry is the two people on my team who don't like screens.
S1.do: Brings in pig-weighing cameras and a pen-washing robot, trains her team in the first six months, and grows consulting to one day a week. Spends some savings on a short farm data course.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some worry for two long-serving staff.
S1.quote: Jakub can tell a sow's about to farrow just by how she's lying. But give him a tablet and he goes quiet.
S1.fieldNote: Priya would automate quickly but carefully, with animal welfare as her limit. Her concern is for staff whose skill is physical and unspoken. She'd fight to keep that skill, though she's also the one bringing in the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's very fast for something with animals in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down where animals are involved. Pig welfare and disease control can't be rushed for anyone's quarterly results. I'd say it at the pig producers' group and to the vets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a better spot than most. Someone has to set up the robots and take responsibility when something goes wrong. But by the end of the two years, I'm not sure even that needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first six months putting in every system that works and learning it inside out. Then I'd sell that experience, either to a big pig company or a tech firm, before everyone else catches up. I've got no kids and no house, so I'd move wherever the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a sharp way. Like the morning of a disease test result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move. Where?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wherever the big pig companies are setting up robot units. Could be another region, could be another country. My sister would be upset, she'd say I always run off. But with two years, you go where the work is, while there's still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the owner and your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the owner first, and help him through it. He's 64, he might just sell. My team, I'd write them the best references I can and push the owner for decent redundancy pay, at least three months each.

S2.say: I'd say slow down where animals are involved, because pig welfare and disease control can't be rushed. I'd say it at the pig producers' group and to the vets.
S2.think: Privately I'm in a better spot than most, because someone has to set up the robots and take responsibility. But by the end of two years, maybe even that won't need a person.
S2.do: Installs and learns every working system in the first six months, then sells that experience to a large pig company or tech firm. Prepares to move region or country for work and pushes her employer to give her team at least three months' redundancy pay.
S2.quote: With two years, you go where the work is, while there's still work.
S2.fieldNote: Priya's response to the fastest picture is to move fast and be mobile, using her lack of ties. She still sets limits around animal welfare in public. She thinks of her team's redundancy pay but accepts that she'll leave them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a proper window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this well, so let's set standards for robots on livestock farms now. Who's responsible when a machine misses a sick pig? I'd want the vets and farmers writing those rules, not just the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is when I'd make the most money. Enough time to build a reputation, not so much that the big firms own everything. Then at the end I'd probably have to change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd turn the consulting into a small business, two days a week, with the owner's blessing. By year two I'd go full-time, setting up robot systems on pig and poultry farms. I'd put about two months of savings into it and keep three back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. I'd probably work too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help you with the business side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister's an office manager, so she'd do the invoices at first. I'd use AI for the rest. It's a small firm, me and maybe one technician, I don't want to build something big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the business when AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably dies, or gets bought. I'd plan for that from the start. Sell in year four if someone offers, and have money in the bank for whatever comes next.

S3.say: I'd say we have time to set standards for robots on livestock farms now, like who's responsible when a machine misses a sick pig. Vets and farmers should write those rules, not just the companies.
S3.think: Privately five years is when I'd make the most money, building a reputation before the big firms own everything. At the end I'd probably have to change again.
S3.do: Turns consulting into a small business two days a week in year one and goes full-time in year two, installing robot systems on pig and poultry farms. Invests about two months of savings, keeps three back, and plans to sell the firm around year four.
S3.feel: Uneasy but excited, and likely to overwork.
S3.quote: Who's responsible when a machine misses a sick pig?
S3.fieldNote: Five years is Priya's ideal window: she'd build and sell a small business within it. She plans the exit from day one, which shows a cool, practical streak. Her public point about responsibility for animal welfare is a thoughtful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to build a career, not just a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to train people properly, so farms should start now. Every pig unit should have one person who really understands the systems. I'd offer to help write the courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine either way. With ten years I'd have time to buy a share in a farm, maybe even this one. That's something I'd never have dreamed of a few years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few years I'd stay at Linden, put in the systems, and keep consulting on the side. Around year three I'd ask the owner about buying into the farm, a small share at first, since he's got no children who want it. I'd keep saving hard, maybe buy a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really. It feels like an opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into the farm. How realistic is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five months of savings, not very, yet. But with ten years, the consulting money, and a bank loan, maybe. The owner's said more than once he wants someone to keep it going. It might be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AGI does arrive in 2036, would owning a farm still make sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think owning the land and the pigs makes more sense than being paid for my time. If machines do the work, the owner still gets the money. I'd rather be the owner than the worker in that picture.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to train people properly, so farms should start now. Every pig unit should have one person who understands the systems, and I'd help write the courses.
S4.think: Privately I'd be fine either way, and with ten years I could buy a share in a farm, maybe this one. I'd never have dreamed of that a few years ago.
S4.do: Stays at Linden, installs the systems and keeps consulting on the side. Around year three asks the owner about buying a small share of the farm, using consulting income and a bank loan, while saving hard and possibly buying a flat.
S4.feel: Calm and excited, as if a door is opening.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the owner than the worker in that picture.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Priya from a mobile consultant into a would-be owner of the farm she runs. Like other farmers in this group, she concludes that ownership beats skill once machines do the work. She sounds energised rather than worried.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not for me but for animals and people. Rushing robots into livestock without rules could mean dead pigs and staff thrown out with nothing. What would help is clear rules on who's responsible for animal welfare when machines run things, and decent redundancy pay for farm staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about disease. If robots move between farms, they can carry disease too. Nobody talks about that, and it could wipe out a unit in a week.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be the owner than the worker in that picture.
portrait: Priya is a 27-year-old pig unit manager on a farm with 700 sows and 350 hectares of grain, who uses AI daily and brought in a cough monitor before anyone else nearby. She's pragmatic, single and mobile, and sees most scenarios as openings rather than threats. Her constant limits are animal welfare and disease control, and she worries for two long-serving staff whose skill doesn't show on a screen. With short warning she'd move wherever the work is; with ten years she'd aim to buy into the farm she runs.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because rushing robots into livestock without rules could harm animals and leave staff with nothing.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules on who is responsible for animal welfare when machines run a farm, and decent redundancy pay for farm staff.
